item.title: AWS Releases a Free Local Emulator of AWS Built Entirely by Agents
item.description:
AWS has released AWS Emulator, a free, CC0-licensed local stand-in for more than 200 of its services, generated from its public API models and aimed at the test loops of coding agents. AWS says agents wrote and maintain all of the code and publishes per-release fidelity scores. The docs say it does not evaluate IAM, and practitioners are split on trusting an emulator nobody reviewed.

By Steef-Jan Wiggers

item.title: Microsoft keeps failing. Why can’t its customers leave?
item.description:
For almost 24 hours last week, millions of Americans lost access to the tools they use to work. A global Microsoft outage knocked out Outlook, Teams and Copilot from Thursday afternoon well into Friday. Congressional work stalled in the middle of a packed lame-duck session. Hospitals, schools, utilities and the agencies that deliver critical services had no way to reach their own staff and, in many cases, no backup. Their only option was to wait while one company repaired its own network.

Microsoft says the cause was a botched network upgrade, not a cyberattack. That is little comfort. Every technology provider has bad days; the test is the consequence. In a competitive market, repeated failure costs a company its customers. For Microsoft, it does not.

Customer captivity is the problem. The outage struck Microsoft’s productivity suite, where its dominance is oldest and deepest, and it reached so far because customers have been steered, by design, into buying everything from one vendor with no practical way out. 

Every Microsoft customer who lost email last week was living with a choice made long ago: by Microsoft, not the customers themselves. It’s central to Microsoft’s business strategy. The company’s licensing is built to make leaving expensive and diversifying impractical. Its dominant productivity software is bundled with communications, security and AI tools, which prices out rivals and limits their access to customers. Customers who want to run Microsoft software on any cloud other than Azure pay more to do so. That’s why a single network failure reached so far: Microsoft’s Defender security screening and the Intune dashboards that administrators use to manage devices went dark along with other services.

This isn’t the first warning. This January, a separate Microsoft 365 outage dragged on for nearly ten hours. In 2025, a global attack exploited a critical SharePoint flaw and breached federal agencies. In 2024, Russian hackers got into Microsoft’s corporate systems and reached internal emails and source code. In 2023, Chinese hackers exploited a flaw in Microsoft’s cloud email service to breach the email accounts of senior U.S. government officials. The federal Cyber Safety Review Board later called Microsoft’s security culture “inadequate” and said it “requires an overhaul.”

Outages and breaches keep happening, and customers keep staying. That is not how a competitive market behaves. The ability to let quality slide without losing customers is a hallmark of monopoly power.

At a 2024 House hearing, Microsoft President Brad Smith said public sector clients “don’t want to switch.” The truth is that they can’t switch easily, because Microsoft’s licensing terms have closed off the exit.

American business leaders tell the same story. In August, the Coalition for Fair Software Licensing surveyed US software and cloud decision-makers:

  • Nine in 10 report at least one concrete harm from Microsoft’s licensing, and 65% report three or more. Harms include a penalty, forced Azure choice, staying on-prem, costly audit, raised prices, AI platform constraint or AI project delay.
  • 83% say Microsoft’s rules meaningfully limit which cloud providers they can realistically consider.
  • 61% of organizations that shopped around chose Azure to avoid fees, not because it was the better product.
  • Eight in ten say they would move workloads away from Azure if the licensing restrictions were lifted.
  • Companies avoid moving to the cloud altogether to avoid Microsoft’s restrictions and increased licensing fees. Two-thirds have kept a workload on their own servers, rather than migrating to the cloud, to dodge restrictive licensing terms.

Microsoft’s costs don’t stay in IT departments. More than half of respondents (56%) raised prices on their own customers to cover higher licensing costs, and a third slowed hiring or cut staff. 

Customers who test the market also pay a price. Respondents who evaluated a competitor were 2.2 times more likely to face a costly audit.

The fix is simple, and customers want it. 94% support letting businesses run software they already own on any cloud without added fees. 86% say federal regulators should examine licensing practices that limit which cloud providers businesses can use.

The FTC is already positioned to deliver. Its inquiry into Microsoft’s licensing has run for two years, and it is probing licensing arrangements, interoperability and potentially exclusionary conduct around Azure. That matters because the licensing that locked customers into one productivity suite is used to pull the rest of their computing onto Microsoft’s cloud. Last week’s outage shows what’s at stake. Market dominance isn’t only a pricing problem. Customers who are free to leave are customers a company has to keep earning. 

Microsoft’s playbook is well established. It apologizes, promises a post-incident report and offers fixes that deepen dependence on its ecosystem. Regulators must refuse to accept this model any longer. The FTC has the evidence, the authority and now a vivid reminder of the cost of doing nothing.

item.title: FAA ground stop offers IT leaders stark modernization lessons
item.description:
A four-plus-hour halt for all US airline flights on Nov. 13, apparently caused by a botched update of telecom equipment, is a high-profile reminder to IT leaders that modernization effects often don’t go as expected and the impact can be severely consequential.

Updating any IT or telecom component without a backup system in place can be risky business, as can scheduling updates during peak system use. In the FAA’s case, the ground stop order came just before 4 p.m. Eastern Time, with about 3,500 flights in the air.

“Peak demand is not the time to discover whether a change was effectively tested,” says Michael Jenkins, CTO at cybersecurity provider ThreatLocker. “Unless waiting creates a greater immediate risk, test, stage, and schedule critical updates for a period when the system can tolerate disruption. Base a maintenance window on operational reality, not convenience.”

IT leaders should consider upgrades during times of lower demand, with enough time to validate the change and restore service before activity increases, agrees Alex Perry, a partner at IT research firm ISG.

“The timing should reflect the potential service impact, even when the task itself is routine,” he says. “Even work that is considered routine can have a significant impact when other systems and services depend on the equipment being changed. A remote location does not necessarily mean the impact will stay local.”

Never a good time

Other IT leaders note that there’s never an optimal time for an organization like the FAA to upgrade its network, with flights happening around the clock. In cases like that, especially with always-on critical systems, a more complex risk calculus is needed,

“You obviously want to avoid introducing unnecessary change during periods of peak business activity,” says Richard Amos, CIO at IT solutions and managed services provider Blue Mantis. “But at some point, delaying change can create more risk than executing the change.”

Eliminating all risk during an IT upgrade is unrealistic, he adds. Instead, IT leaders should focus on understanding and managing the risk, and making deliberate decisions about the level of risk the organization is willing to accept, he says.

Details are sketchy

Nearly a week after the FAA incident, the exact cause of the ground stop ordered remains unknown, with officials from President Donald Trump’s administration alternatively saying it was related to a replacement of copper telecom wiring, replacement of a router, or a software upgrade.

Supposedly, when a new router was connected to the FAA network at a “remote” location in Arkansas, it began to flood the national air traffic communications network with about 1,000 connection attempts every four to five seconds, effectively creating an internal DDoS attack.

Despite the ongoing confusion about the cause of the incident, most IT leaders see a pressing need for the FAA to update its decades-old, copper-based telecom network. But IT modernization efforts rarely go exactly as planned, they say.

Instead of episodic modernization efforts, organizations should consider lifecycle management plans, Blue Mantis’ Amos advises. IT leaders should maintain accurate asset inventories and understand end-of-life and end-of-support dates, he says.

However, decades-old technology isn’t necessarily bad technology, he adds.

“If something has been engineered for reliability and continues to perform its intended function, its age alone isn’t sufficient reason to replace it,” Amos says. “The problem tends to be security, support, recovery, and dependencies — in other words, the risk accumulating around it.”

That said, organizations may be ignoring significant risks if they ignore IT upgrades because the current system works, he adds.

“‘If it ain’t broke, don’t fix it’ can work for your toaster, but it is not a technology strategy,” Amos says. “At the same time, you shouldn’t modernize simply because something new is available, or bright and shiny. Modernization should be tied to a business outcome like reducing risk, increasing resiliency, improving security, lowering cost, and such.”

In addition to the timing of upgrades, another major lesson from the FAA ground stop is to test and the proposed fixes and to have backup systems in place, says Joe Saunders, founder and CEO of cybersecurity vendor RunSafe Security.

“The biggest lesson is that modernization isn’t just about replacing old hardware or migrating to newer software,” he says. “It’s about building resilience into the entire system.”

Before major upgrades, IT leaders need to understand how different technologies interact, identify potential points of failure, and ensure that a problem in one area doesn’t cascade across operations, Saunders advises.

“Critical infrastructure operators should be planning not only for upgrades, but also for continuity when those upgrades don’t go exactly as expected,” he adds. “Resilience has to be treated as a core requirement, not an afterthought.”

Replacing old systems can become necessary, but IT leaders should focus on incremental upgrades, extensive testing, parallel operations where possible, and architectures that limit the impact of any single failure, Saunders recommends.

“Critical systems can’t remain frozen in time indefinitely,” he says. “Older technology often becomes harder to support, maintain, and secure as expertise, replacement parts, and vendor support diminishes.”

Evaluate risks and rewards

The “ain’t broke” approach to IT systems maintenance can be seductive for the bottom line, and even work for a while, but IT leaders should use the FAA ground stop and other high-profile outages of late as stark reminders to CEOs and their boards that infrastructure upgrades are necessary and must be invested in and planned for well in advance, instead of waiting until a system reaches a crisis point before taking action or rushing through modernization to capitalize quickly on technology advances.

“There’s some truth to the idea that proven systems can be highly reliable, especially in safety-critical environments where stability matters,” Saunders says. “The challenge is that ‘not broken’ doesn’t necessarily mean sustainable or secure over the long term.”

ISG’s Perry notes that modernization often happens incrementally, with new equipment and software introduced alongside older technology. IT leaders should check how the old and new technology will work together. Before work begins, the technical team and contractors should agree on the potential impact, who can authorize or stop the change, and how operations will continue if something goes wrong, he recommends.

“You need the right technical staff, vendor support, and people with authority to make decisions if service is disrupted,” Perry adds. “The window has to allow time for recovery from a failed change, as well as installation. A quiet period that ends just before a critical business deadline may leave very little room to respond.”

item.title: The dark side of AI in hiring: When job applicants become security threats
item.description:
Employers have always dealt with job applicants who stretch the truth. Candidates exaggerate their technical skills, embellish their experience or take too much credit for accomplishments. Hiring managers have learned to expect some résumé inflation. AI has changed the nature and scale of the problem.

According to recent research, a cell of up to 22 North Korean operatives submitted nearly 167,000 job applications in roughly nine months using stolen identities, AI-assisted interviewing and US-based stand-ins. It landed more than 21,000 interviews and secured at least 76 job offers.

As evidenced, employers aren’t simply dealing with candidates overblowing their qualifications. They’re confronting applicants who fabricate entire professional histories, assume false identities, manipulate screening processes and secure jobs under fraudulent pretenses.

Deception that was once an individual act of “putting your best self forward” can now be automated and executed at scale, and the consequences extend beyond a bad hire. For tech and HR leaders, the hiring process is becoming a new enterprise attack surface.

Résumé inflation meets industrial-scale deception

AI has dramatically lowered the barriers to creating convincing job applications. An applicant can generate a résumé that aligns almost perfectly with a job description, complete with the right technical skills, certifications and accomplishments, regardless of whether those qualifications are real.

Using AI to improve a résumé or tailor it to a role is reasonable. Using AI to invent experience, qualifications or entire professional identities is a different problem. It may sound dramatic, but it’s happening now, and we’re not just talking about isolated bad actors.

Consider an employer hiring for a specialized technology role. Its applicant tracking system identifies 10 candidates whose résumés match 95% or more of the job requirements. On paper, all appear exceptionally qualified. But what if nine have fabricated substantial portions of their experience?

Some of those matches are honest. Tailoring a résumé to a role is smart. But copying the job description is not experience. The difference is job description mirroring: language lifted from the posting with no evidence of the work behind it.

Employers face two competing risks: advancing fraudulent candidates or becoming so suspicious of perfect matches that they reject the one genuinely exceptional applicant. This is the new challenge of AI-driven applicant fraud: detecting sophisticated deception without penalizing (or missing out on) legitimate talent.

From fake applicants to legitimate security threats

The most troubling evolution of applicant fraud involves individuals deliberately attempting to gain access to organizations through fraudulent employment. This is where the issue moves from talent acquisition to cybersecurity.

In April 2026, the Department of Justice announced the sentencing of two individuals who helped North Korean IT workers obtain remote employment at more than 100 American companies using at least 80 stolen identities. The operation generated more than $5 million in illicit revenue and gave fraudulent workers access to sensitive company information and source code, including export-controlled defense-related data. Cases like this demonstrate a dangerous bypassing of conventional cybersecurity defenses.

Organizations spend significant resources preventing unauthorized outsiders from accessing their networks. Yet a malicious actor who successfully navigates the hiring process may receive legitimate credentials, corporate equipment and access to proprietary systems. In other words, the call is coming from inside the house.

For CIOs and CISOs, this raises an uncomfortable question: How much confidence can an organization place in its access controls if the identity of the person receiving those permissions was never properly vetted?

Traditional screening is no longer enough

Most hiring systems were designed to evaluate qualifications, not investigate sophisticated identity fraud. Applicant tracking systems excel at matching keywords and ranking candidates against job requirements. But these capabilities become liabilities when malicious applicants understand how to manipulate them.

Even detecting AI-generated résumés is harder than it sounds. Technical characteristics of a résumé file, including metadata and document-generation methods, can sometimes reveal unusual production patterns. But no single signal proves fraud. A legitimate candidate might use AI to polish a résumé. A malicious applicant can edit fabricated content by hand to make it look authentic.

A recent investigation by security company Pindrop illustrates why patterns matter. In October, the company reported discovering one identity associated with three applicants, overlapping phone numbers, similar résumés, inconsistent employment histories and suspicious document metadata. It also described an incident in which someone other than the expected candidate joined an interview. Individually, some of these anomalies might have innocent explanations. Together, they warrant investigation.

Simply uploading a résumé to a chatbot and asking whether it’s real won’t solve the problem. AI can’t reliably verify an applicant’s identity or employment history from the document alone. The answer is a more sophisticated approach to evaluating authenticity.

Hiring needs a fraud-detection mindset

Financial institutions have spent decades developing systems to detect suspicious transactions without automatically blocking every unusual purchase. Employers need a similar philosophy.

Rather than relying on a single indicator, organizations should evaluate multiple signals throughout hiring: inconsistent professional histories, suspicious similarities across applications, discrepancies between claimed and demonstrated expertise, unusual document provenance and evidence of interview impersonation.

The FBI warned in October that North Korean IT workers increasingly use facilitators to participate in interviews, verify fraudulent identities and manage employer-issued devices. The agency recommends an approach it calls “identity in depth,” combining verification and detection throughout the employment lifecycle.

This is an important distinction. An unusually strong résumé isn’t proof of fraud. Neither is using generative AI. Employers that treat these characteristics as inherently suspicious risk excluding qualified applicants. Effective detection requires corroborating evidence, human review and safeguards against false positives.

The CIO’s role in securing hiring

Historically, hiring technology has been HR’s responsibility. But as fraudulent applications become more sophisticated, CIOs must become active participants in protecting the process.

First, candidate authenticity should be treated as an enterprise risk. HR, IT, cybersecurity and compliance teams need shared procedures for identifying suspicious activity and investigating potential fraud.

Second, verification must extend beyond the résumé. Employers need to verify that candidates are who they claim to be, that applications reflect their capabilities and experience, and that the individual hired is the person who completed screening.

Third, identity assurance shouldn’t end when an offer is signed. Secure onboarding, appropriate background checks and least-privilege access controls can limit the damage caused by a fraudulent hire.

Finally, organizations must resist replacing human judgment with opaque AI fraud scores. Detection systems should inform decisions, not make them. Every flag should come with an explanation a recruiter can review, and no candidate should be rejected on an ambiguous indicator alone.

In a world where trust can no longer be assumed, the goal isn’t to treat candidates like suspects, but to confirm their authenticity.

item.title: AI leadership: 3 success lessons from CBA’s chief AI officer
item.description:
These are early, fascinating days for the corporate title du jour — chief artificial intelligence officer (CAIO).

So when the CAIO of Australia’s largest bank, Commonwealth Bank (CBA), stands up to talk about his role and how times are changing, it’s worth a closer look.

I recently interviewed Ranil Boteju, CBA’s CAIO, on stage at Momentum Media’s FST Future of Financial Services, Data & AI conference, and one of his answers pointed to the story behind the story.

“I am the chief AI officer, but I’m one of many.” The real chief AI officer, he said, is “our CEO.”

Every organization is different, but it points to an early dilemma for CAIOs. Who, exactly, should be in charge of this AI transformation movement? CFOs, CMOs, CIOs and even CISOs have a stake, and the benefit is well-documented roles with clear areas of responsibility.

And of course, as Boteju notes, the CEO is key. If CEOs don’t ‘get it,’ the organization has bigger problems.

Mark Jones, The Story Code Co.

CAIOs finding their feet

Keep that tension in mind because Boteju’s experience offers plenty of lessons for companies forging an AI transformation path.

CAIOs occupy a rare space in the race to AI adoption: they’re highly influential and respected yet hold varying degrees of authority. Boteju does run a centre of excellence and builds the shared capabilities the business draws on, but if we step back, he still has a structural problem.

Like chief digital officers before him — a parallel he drew himself — Boteju holds a role that champions a technology which creates value only when it’s embedded across the entire business. “The chief digital officer was a digital team, and they were doing digital, and everyone was by definition not digital,” he said. The lesson he took from that era is noteworthy: “AI transformation can’t be constrained to one team.”

Clearly he’s not responsible for a vertical silo like his C-suite peers and, I’d add, necessarily so. Each business unit should “really lead their agenda”, he said, underpinned by “a common set of capabilities that I would build”.

CAIOs must master managing up to their CEO, collaborating sideways across the C-suite and providing the top-down inspiration that helps whole teams embrace and extend the vision for AI transformation.

So, what’s his story?

All this is vital because it shapes how leaders should understand his story. I picked up three lessons from his talk and our conversation.

1. Context is your moat

Before your buzzword filter goes off, this insight is worth a closer look. When everyone has relatively equal access to the same AI technologies, or at least the same large language models, it pays to understand how your competitive moat is changing.

“In a world where all of the banks are using the same models, what will differentiate us is the context, the organizational memory, all of the tacit knowledge that sits in people’s heads,” Boteju said. “This is effectively our moat.”

That’s the scarce, underused asset inside most companies: what your people know but have never written down. The patterns they’ve recognized over time, and their hard-earned wisdom. A standard operating process, he noted, “is pretty high-level. A lot of it sits in people’s heads.”

Of course, some of this knowledge can also be found scattered throughout vast collections of unstructured data in all organizations. But his point is that analysis isn’t the gap. Asked when data is good enough, he said that in most financial services organizations “there is no excuse to wait”.

So, here’s the better question: how much of what your organization knows has been written down, and how much of it could you hand to an agent tomorrow?

2. Simplify your strategy

Oh, how we love to overcomplicate enterprise IT strategies! And yet Boteju stood on stage with clean, simple slides that broke down his strategic thinking.

“The reason for doing AI needs to be really clear in your organization,” he said. “We’re not jumping on a bandwagon.”

CBA has chosen four strategic priorities: customer experience, fraud and scams, faster delivery and reimagining work. Each one makes sense, so that begs the next question: how can AI deliver against each of these easily understood priorities at scale?

The answer for CBA is five enablers, also presented on one slide: one AI platform, an AI control plane, token optimization, context and knowledge, and skills and capabilities.

Mark Jones, The Story Code Co.

The alternative is a familiar story to anyone in this game. A few years ago, he said, it was “1,000 flowers blooming, lots of duplication, lots of POCs, nothing really scaled.” His advice now is to have “a really narrow set of … use cases to focus on”. Could you put your AI strategy on one page?

3. AI transformation is a control game

This point is a meta-insight I took from CBA’s big picture. Think about the dominant AI industry narrative pushed by the LLM leaders in particular: you can’t control AI — heck, even we can’t control agents and we built them!

Now contrast that with Boteju’s approach, which he describes as “machine layers of defence”. “We register every single asset,” he said. “Any given moment, I can point to all of the AI agents that are underway, live in production or being built.” Nothing goes live unless it passes pre-deployment testing. Then, in his words: “Has there been any drift? Is there anything that we need to be concerned about? We can monitor that in real time.” Outcomes are checked after the fact, and an independent team validates the lot.

Know what you can control and what you can’t — and have a plan for both.

And look back at the five enablers for a moment. Maintaining control is a strategy that runs through most of them: the AI platform and control plane, token spend (a single gateway, caps for engineers and smaller, cheaper models for less intensive tasks), and how context is protected. “To pick out the one thing at the bank that we need to really protect,” he said, “it’s our context and knowledge.” The final enabler is a handy $90m, which he said CBA is investing in upskilling teams.

In short, this is the behaviour of an organization that’s not lying down and letting the AI juggernaut run over it.

What’s your story?

It’s often said, “comparison is the thief of joy” — but in this case it should be an opportunity for inspiration and pointed reflection.

What comes to mind when you look at CBA’s approach and then hold up a mirror? You might have a CAIO who’s been given all the responsibility and none of the authority. Or perhaps your organization lacks the clarity of strategic thinking clearly evident at CBA?

As always, success is not contingent on one C-suite title, but on how your entire team understands and communicates the story of change that’s required in times like these. Times when new titles come and go, change feels faster than ever, and clarity can feel like a distant dream enjoyed by others.

In my mind, it starts with challenging the control narrative. Are you living inside your own story, or the AI industry’s adopted fear, uncertainty and doubt (FUD) narrative?

item.title: Discord Rewrites Desktop and Mobile Clients in Rust Using Zed's GPU-Accelerated Rendering Framework
item.description:
Discord’s CTO Stanislav Vishnevskiy recently announced rewriting its desktop and mobile clients in Rust, moving away from Electron and React Native. The project eliminates layers of abstraction to directly leverage the device’s GPU, native mobile views, and a Rust core shared across platforms. Early results hint at a significant reduction in RAM usage and boot time for chat, voice, and streaming.

By Bruno Couriol
